plate_findings.evidence: A 10 × 11 mm red dome-shaped nodule above the anterior part of the left ear

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Clinical photograph of a human patient showing a red dome-shaped nodule immediately anterior to the left ear. The in-text explicitly attributes the lesion to epithelioid hemangioma (angiolymphoid hyperplasia with eosinophilia): a 40-year-old man with this periauricular nodule whose biopsy showed dilated dermal vessels, plump endothelial cells and eosinophil-rich infiltrate. Periauricular papulonodules are the classic presentation of ALHE, and the panel is a real, clear patient image with no third-party indicator. b: Enlarged clinical photograph of the same periauricular lesion shown in panel a, from a patient whose biopsy confirmed epithelioid hemangioma (angiolymphoid hyperplasia with eosinophilia). The lesion is a red dome-shaped nodule in the classic periauricular distribution of ALHE; the image is a real patient photograph, well lit, with visible light skin and no third-party indicator.

in_text_mentions: A 40-year-old man noticed a 10 × 11 mm red dome-shaped nodule above the anterior part of the left ear for over a year (Figure 4a,b). There were no subjective symptoms, and excisional biopsy revealed dilated blood vessels in all layers of the dermis and enlarged endothelial cells lining blood vessels (Figure 5a,b). In addition, inflammatory cell infiltration with few eosinophils was observed in the surrounding area (Figure 5c), which led to the diagnosis of EH. After the resection, the patient passed without any problems.

Caption explicitly describes prominent vascular proliferation with swollen endothelial cells at the edge of a germinal center, and in-text confirms pithelioid endothelial cells protruding into the lumen with eosinophil-rich perivascular infiltrate, leading to the ALHE diagnosis. Both key histologic features of ALHE are directly supported by caption and in-text evidence.

There was an interstitial and perivascular infiltrate composed primarily of histiocytes and eosinophils with secondary lymphoid follicles (Figs. 2, 3 &4). in_text_mentions: Microscopic examination (Figures 2(A), 2(B), 2(C), and 2(D)) of the tonsil revealed a dense inflammatory cell infiltrate consisting largely of plasmacytoid lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils. There was exocytosis of eosinophils into the overlying squamous mucosa and vascular proliferation comprising of numerous thin‐walled capillary‐sized vessels arranged in a lobular pattern. Foci of necrosis were present, some of which were centered around blood vessels, but there was no vasculitis. The B‐ and T‐cell markers were of a benign mixed pattern, excluding a lymphoproliferative process.

The caption explicitly attributes this to an epithelioid hemangioma (EH), the entity mapped to the configured ALHE spectrum, and describes the bright T1 signal as a classic radiological finding reflecting high vascularity. b: Axial T2 Dixon MRI of the same human-patient lesion (arrow), showing a gray (solid, cellular) signal rather than a cyst. panels.attribution_text: Moens et al. Epithelioid Hemangioma of the External Auditory Canal: A Case Report.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.115593. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Imaging findings of an EH (see arrows) The MRI appearance of an EH as bright (white) on Gd T1 Dixon opp (a) and gray on T2 Dixon in (b) is a classic radiological finding. The bright signal on T1 reflects the intense contrast enhancement (Gd) due to the tumor’s high vascularity. Meanwhile, the gray signal on T2 indicates a solid, cellular tumor rather than a simple fluid-filled cyst or a common cavernous hemangioma. This combination confirms a highly vascularized, solid soft-tissue mass. On an arteriogram, an EH typically presents as a hypervascular mass with an intense and prolonged tumoral blush, enlarged feeding arteries, and dense capillary staining, which outlines the solid, cellular nature of the mass (c). EH, epithelioid hemangioma
in_text_mentions: al and venous components, characterized by rapid arterial flow and systolic-diastolic modulations. Selective arteriography was subsequently performed. This showed a highly vascularized tumor supplied exclusively by a hypertrophied right posterior auricular artery. A dense arteriocapillary network with early venous drainage and a nodular appearance was noted. Although the vascular pattern raised the possibility of an arteriovenous malformation (AVM), the solitary arterial supply coupled with the nodular architecture was more suggestive of a hypervascular tumor rather than a true AVM (Figure 1).

MRI was conducted to assess the extent of the lesion. It confirmed the invasion of the right external auditory canal, concha, and antihelix, with a moderately hypointense signal on both T1- and T2-weighted sequences, along with marked contrast enhancement. The lesion measured 28 mm × 16 mm × 29 mm (transverse×anteroposterior×craniocaudal). Importantly, no abnormalities were detected in the regional lymph nodes; the parotid area and levels IIa and IIb all presented with subcentimeter lymph nodes (Figure 1).

source_variant.figure_caption: a Skin masses observed on the base of the left thumb and on the volar side of the index finger. b Magnetic resonance imaging of the lesion (red arrows) on the dorsal side of the thumb showed isointensity in T1-weighted images and high intensity in T2-weighted images. The tumor was confined to the skin. c Increase in the number of blood vessels in the dermal layer and eosinophilic infiltrates were noted around vascular endothelial cells.
